introduction-why-client-side-hooks-arent.core: Client-side hooks are optional: they aren't cloned by default and can be skipped with --no-verify. Server-side hooks run on the central repository and can't be bypassed, so policy is enforced there.

first_principles.problem: Secrets and force-pushes reach main because someone never installed the pre-commit hook or skipped it.
truths: The server is the single point every push passes through.
Policy must be unavoidable to be reliable.
derivation: Use **server hooks / platform rules** for enforcement.
Enforce **secrets, branch, size and message** policies on the server.

analogy.title: A sign in the parking lot vs. a bouncer at the door
analogy.story: Anyone can ignore the sign; nobody gets past the bouncer.
analogy.breaks: Server hooks give feedback late (at push time), so keep client hooks for the fast loop.

example.title: A leaked AWS key

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Enforcement belongs where it can't be skipped.

example.outcome: policy is guaranteed, not hoped for.

check.q: Why can't client-side hooks enforce policy?
check.a: They aren't distributed automatically and can be bypassed with --no-verify.

the-three-server-side-hooks-and-when-the.core: A push runs three server hooks in sequence: pre-receive (once, sees all refs, can reject everything), update (once per ref, can reject that ref) and post-receive (after success, can't reject, runs automation).

first_principles.problem: Putting logic in the wrong hook means it either can't block bad pushes or runs too late.
truths: A push updates possibly many refs.
Rejection must happen before refs move.
Side effects should run only after success.

analogy.title: Airport security stages
analogy.story: The main screening (pre-receive), gate-specific checks (update) and baggage tracking after boarding (post-receive).
analogy.breaks: Long-running hooks delay every push, so keep them fast.

example.title: A push of two branches

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Any non-zero exit before the update stops the push.

example.outcome: logic goes in the right stage.

check.q: Which server hook can't reject a push?

the-pre-receive-hook-the-main-gate.core: pre-receive reads `old new ref` lines on stdin for every ref in the push. A non-zero exit rejects the whole push atomically, and its stderr messages are shown to the pusher.

first_principles.problem: You need one place to scan every new commit for secrets, oversized files or bad messages before anything lands.
truths: New objects are quarantined until the hook passes.
One rejection blocks every ref in the push.
The pusher sees the hook's output.
derivation: List the new commits with **git rev-list old..new**.
**Exit 1** with a clear message to reject.

analogy.title: A customs inspection of a whole shipment
analogy.story: If one crate has contraband, the entire shipment is turned back.
analogy.breaks: Handle new branches (old = 000…) and deletions (new = 000…) explicitly.

example.title: Blocking AWS keys

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The push fails with a clear reason, and nothing lands.

code.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
zero=0000000000000000000000000000000000000000
while read old new ref; do
  [ "$new" = "$zero" ] && continue
  range=$([ "$old" = "$zero" ] && echo "$new" || echo "$old..$new")
  if git log -p "$range" | grep -qE 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}'; then
    echo "Rejected: AWS access key found in $ref" >&2; exit 1
  fi
done

example.outcome: one airtight gate for all pushes.

check.q: What does pre-receive receive on stdin?
check.a: One line per ref: old SHA, new SHA and ref name.

the-update-hook-per-branch-policy.core: The update hook runs once per ref with arguments (refname, old, new), so you can apply different rules per branch: block force-pushes to main, restrict release/* to certain users, and so on. Only that ref is rejected.

first_principles.problem: Policy differs by branch: feature branches can be rewritten, main must never be.
derivation: Detect a **force-push**: `git merge-base --is-ancestor old new` fails.
**Exit non-zero** to reject just this ref.

analogy.title: Different locks on different doors
analogy.story: The staff room has a code lock, the vault a biometric one, and the lobby is open.
analogy.breaks: Per-ref hooks run more often, so keep them fast for pushes with many refs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Feature branches can still be force-pushed, but main can't.

code.text:
ref=$1 old=$2 new=$3
if [ "$ref" = refs/heads/main ] && ! git merge-base --is-ancestor "$old" "$new"; then
  echo "Force-push to main is not allowed" >&2; exit 1
fi

check.q: How can a hook detect a force-push?
check.a: The old SHA isn't an ancestor of the new SHA (merge-base --is-ancestor fails).

the-post-receive-hook-triggering-automat.core: post-receive runs after refs are updated. It can't reject anything, but it's the place for side effects: triggering CI and deploys, sending notifications, mirroring and updating caches.

first_principles.problem: Automation should run only for pushes that actually succeeded.
truths: Once refs are updated the change is final.
Side effects shouldn't block the pusher.
Failures here don't undo the push.
derivation: Read the same **old new ref** stdin.
**Trigger** CI or deploy webhooks for matching branches.
Run slow work **asynchronously** (enqueue rather than block).

analogy.title: The announcement after a vote passes
analogy.story: Once the vote is final, the clerk notifies everyone and starts the follow-up work.
analogy.breaks: Errors in post-receive can't roll back the push, so make the automation robust.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every successful push to main deploys automatically.

code.text:
while read old new ref; do
  if [ "$ref" = refs/heads/main ]; then
    curl -fsS -X POST "$DEPLOY_HOOK" -d "sha=$new" &
  fi
done

check.q: Why can't post-receive reject a push?
check.a: It runs after the refs are already updated, so the push is final.

modern-platforms-push-rules-and-branch-p.core: On GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket Cloud you can't install raw hooks. The same enforcement comes from branch protection and rulesets, push rules, secret scanning push protection, required status checks and webhooks.

first_principles.problem: Cloud-hosted repositories have no accessible hooks/ directory, so policy needs another mechanism.
truths: Hosted platforms abstract away the server.
derivation: **Branch protection / rulesets**: no force-push, require PR reviews.
**Push rules** (GitLab): commit message regex, file size.

analogy.title: A managed building with a security desk
analogy.story: You can't rewire the locks yourself, but the security company enforces your access rules.
analogy.breaks: Platform rules are less flexible than arbitrary scripts, so custom checks move into required CI jobs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The same guarantees as server hooks, with no server access.

check.q: What replaces post-receive hooks on GitHub?
check.a: Webhooks and GitHub Actions triggered by push events.
